questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Choosing a translation strategy from a three-way cost model, where the compiler and the interpreter cross at a value of N that is never on the cheapest frontier
questions.challenge_mechanism: The cheapest of the three strategies is not the one that wins any single pairwise comparison. The compiler and the interpreter do cross, and the crossover is real arithmetic, but at the value of N where it happens the bytecode build is cheaper than both, so that crossover never appears on the cheapest frontier at all. A candidate who computes crossovers in pairs and reports each one as a segment of the answer produces a frontier with a piece in it that does not exist, and the piece is wrong in the direction that looks most plausible.
questions.question:
A laboratory writes a data-reduction tool that has to run on the three operating systems its collaborators use. The team can distribute the tool in any of three forms. In form A the source is compiled ahead of time into a native executable, and one executable has to be built and tested for each of the three systems. In form B the source is shipped as it stands and translated every time the tool is run. In form C the source is compiled once, on the laboratory's own machine, into bytecode, and that single bytecode build is shipped to all three systems and executed there by a bytecode interpreter.

The figure gives the total cost of each form, in arbitrary cost units, as a function of N, the number of times the tool is executed in total across all three systems. A dashed line marks the number of executions the team currently expects. The costs are the whole cost of owning each form: translation, distribution and execution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the value of N at which forms B and C have the same total cost, and state which of the two forms is cheaper immediately below that value and which is cheaper immediately above it. Show the equation you solved.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the value of N at which forms C and A have the same total cost. Hence state, for each of the three forms, the range of N over which that form is the cheapest of the three. Where a boundary of your range is a tie rather than a strict win, say so.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The team's current estimate is the value of N marked on the figure. Determine the total cost of each of the three forms at that estimate, and state the saving the cheapest form makes against the next cheapest. A colleague recommends form A for every project because it has the lowest cost per execution. Explain why a comparison of forms A and B on their own would have supported that recommendation at this estimate, and state the smallest number of executions at which the recommendation would actually change. Reach a judgement on which form the team should ship.

questions.answer:
(a) The figure gives the three cost models directly: form A is $1200 + 4N$, form B is $20N$, and form C is $240 + 8N$, all in the same cost units. Forms B and C are equal when $20N = 240 + 8N$, so $12N = 240$ and $N = 20$ (M1). At that value both cost $400$ (A1). Immediately below 20 the coefficient of $N$ is smaller for B than for C, so B is cheaper: at $N = 19$, B costs $380$ and C costs $392$. Immediately above 20, C is cheaper: at $N = 21$, B costs $420$ and C costs $408$ (A1).

(b) Forms C and A are equal when $240 + 8N = 1200 + 4N$, so $4N = 960$ and $N = 240$ (M1). At that value both cost $2160$ (A1).

The three ranges are found by taking the lower of the three costs at each N, not by listing the pairwise crossovers.

- Form B is the cheapest for $N \leq 19$. At $N = 20$ B and C are tied at $400$.
- Form C is the cheapest for $21 \leq N \leq 239$. At $N = 240$ C and A are tied at $2160$.
- Form A is the cheapest for $N \geq 241$. At $N = 241$, A costs $2164$ and C costs $2168$ (A1).

Two of the three boundaries are therefore ties rather than wins (A1).

(c) At the estimate marked on the figure, $N = 100$. Form A costs $1200 + 400 = 1600$; form B costs $2000$; form C costs $240 + 800 = 1040$ (M1). Form C is the cheapest, and the saving against the next cheapest, which is form A, is $1600 - 1040 = 560$ cost units (A1).

The colleague's recommendation is not unreasonable when only A and B are considered. Forms A and B are equal when $1200 + 4N = 20N$, so $N = 75$, and A is cheaper than B for every $N$ above 75 (M1). At an estimate of 100, which is above 75, a comparison of those two forms alone therefore recommends A, and the recommendation is supported by the arithmetic of that comparison. It is still the wrong recommendation, because the question is not which of A and B is cheaper but which of the three is cheapest. At $N = 75$ form A and form B both cost $1500$, while form C costs $840$ (A1). The crossover at 75 is a genuine crossover, and it is not on the cheapest frontier: at every value of N the frontier passes through, form C is below both of the strategies that cross there. Reporting the crossover at 75 as a boundary of the answer puts a segment into the frontier that does not exist, and it does so in the direction that looks most plausible, because A really is cheaper than B above 75 (A1).

The recommendation changes at $N = 241$, which is the smallest number of executions for which form A is the cheapest of the three (A1). Below that, form C is cheaper. So the estimate would have to be wrong by more than a factor of two, in the direction of more executions, before the colleague's recommendation became the right one.

The judgement is that the team should ship form C at the current estimate (A1). Form C costs $1040$ against $1600$ for form A, a saving of $560$ cost units, or thirty-five per cent of form A's total. It also keeps the property that made form A attractive in the first place, since a single bytecode build is produced once and then runs on all three systems, so no per-system build or test effort is needed. The judgement is not unconditional: it holds while the estimate stays below 241 executions. If the tool is later executed far more often than expected, the per-execution cost of $8$ for form C against $4$ for form A becomes decisive, and form A becomes the cheaper choice. A recommendation that is not attached to the estimate it was made for is not a recommendation, it is a preference (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) 3 marks. One mark for setting $20N = 240 + 8N$ and reaching $N = 20$. One mark for stating that B is cheaper below 20 and C is cheaper above it. One mark for a justification that uses the per-execution coefficients rather than a restatement of the figure.

(b) 4 marks. One mark for solving $240 + 8N = 1200 + 4N$ to $N = 240$. One mark for the range over which C is cheapest, which must run from 21 to 239. One mark for the range over which A is cheapest, which must begin at 241 and not at 240. One mark for recognising that $N = 20$ and $N = 240$ are ties, so both boundaries are stated as equal costs rather than as wins. A candidate who writes 'A is cheapest for $N > 240$' has the right boundary and should keep the mark, provided the ranges do not overlap.

A candidate who reports three ranges taken from the three pairwise crossovers, that is B below 20, C from 21 to 75 and A above 76, has computed every crossover correctly and has still produced a frontier that does not exist. Award at most two of the four marks and read part (c) before deciding the second.

(c) 6 marks. One mark for the three totals at $N = 100$: 1600, 2000 and 1040. One mark for the saving of 560 against the next cheapest, which is A and not B. One mark for locating the A and B crossover at 75 and showing that it is above the estimate. One mark for the observation that form C undercuts both strategies at that crossover, which is what removes the segment from the frontier. One mark for the change point at 241. One mark for a judgement on form C that is attached to the estimate, and that names the condition under which it would change. A bare 'ship form C because it is cheaper' earns the first four marks and not the last two.

Accept a candidate who notes that the figure's costs are the whole cost of owning each form, so the per-system build effort is already inside form A's fixed cost and must not be added again.

A candidate who answers part (c) with 'form A, because 100 is greater than 75' has answered the two-form question. This is the trap, and it must not be credited as an evaluation of the three-form choice.
questions.explanation:
This item is about the difference between a comparison and an optimisation. Any two linear cost models cross once, so there are three crossovers among three forms: A and B at 75, B and C at 20, and A and C at 240. Each is real arithmetic and each can be found by setting the two expressions equal. The cheapest form at a given N, however, is the minimum of the three, and a crossover between two strategies is only a boundary of that minimum if neither of them is beaten by the third at that value. At $N = 75$ the third form costs $840$ while the two that cross both cost $1500$, so the boundary at 75 is not a boundary of the minimum at all.

The A and B crossover is the trap because it is the one a candidate is most likely to compute. The colleague's claim in part (c) is written to invite exactly that computation: 'the lowest cost per execution' is true of form A, the comparison with form B is the one the claim invites, and at an estimate of 100 the comparison gives the colleague the right answer. Everything the candidate is told points at A, and the figure contradicts it.

The item also carries the two tie points, at $N = 20$ and $N = 240$, where two forms cost exactly the same. They matter because they fix the boundaries of the ranges: C is cheapest from 21 and not from 20, and A is cheapest from 241 and not from 240. A candidate who writes the boundaries as strict inequalities in the wrong direction creates a gap or an overlap at each tie, and part (b) asks for the ties to be named so that this is visible in the answer rather than hidden in it.

Finally, the item is an evaluation rather than a calculation because the arithmetic does not by itself say which form to ship. Form C is cheaper at the estimate and it preserves the single-build property that form A was chosen for; form A is cheaper per execution and wins if the estimate is badly wrong. The judgement mark is for attaching the recommendation to the estimate it was made for, which is the same discipline the guide asks for when it requires the use-cases of each translation approach to be considered.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: a cross-platform distribution decision, in which the three forms differ in where the translation happens and how many build artefacts are produced, rather than an exercise that compares two translation strategies on a single machine. Given and asked: the three cost models are given only inside a figure, and the candidate is asked for the range over which each form is cheapest rather than for a single crossover. Reasoning chain: the final part requires the candidate to reject a pairwise comparison that the data supports, which is only possible once the three-way frontier has been separated from the three pairwise crossovers.
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-level Computer Science and US AP Computer Science A: compilers and interpreters, translation against execution cost, and the portability of bytecode (structure adapted; all coefficients, the three-form framing and the frontier argument are original)

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Find the crossover of each pair of cost models by setting the two expressions equal, then report the three crossovers as the three boundaries of the cheapest strategy, giving the ranges as below 20, from 21 to 75, and above 76
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: A pairwise crossover is a boundary of the cheapest strategy only when the third strategy does not beat both of the crossing pair there. At N equal to 75 the two crossing forms both cost 1500 while the bytecode form costs 840, so the crossover at 75 is not on the frontier and the segment it would create does not exist
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Form B cheapest to 19, form C from 21 to 75, form A from 76 upward, with the recommendation for a hundred executions given as form A because the estimate lies above the A and B crossover at 75

verification.method: The three cost models are evaluated at every integer N from 0 to 400 and the argmin is taken with ties retained, so the frontier is enumerated rather than derived; the two tie points are then confirmed by solving each pair directly. The totals at the estimate are recomputed from the models and checked against the figure's coefficients.
solution_skeleton: Read the three cost expressions out of the figure legend.
Solve each pair of expressions for equality to locate the three crossovers.
Take the minimum of the three at each N to obtain the cheapest frontier.
Discard the A and B crossover at 75 because the bytecode form beats both there.
Evaluate the three totals at the estimate and compare against the next cheapest.
Attach the recommendation to the estimate and state where it would change.

questions.syllabus_ref: A2.4 Network security (A2.4.1 discuss the effectiveness of firewalls at protecting a network, including the function of firewalls in inspecting and filtering incoming and outgoing traffic based on whitelists, blacklists and rules, and the strengths and limitations of firewalls)
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A rule-based packet filter in which one rule is unreachable because a broader rule with the same destination pattern is evaluated first
questions.challenge_mechanism: The rule that mentions SSH is present, correct and in the table, and it has never decided anything. A rule is only evaluated when every rule above it has failed to match, and the rule above it matches a destination pattern that contains the one this rule matches, with every other field left as a wildcard. So the flow the rule was written for is decided by the rule above it, and the administrator's intent is defeated by a rule that is doing exactly what it was written to do.
questions.question:
A small research institute has three networks. Its staff work from the internet, its system administrators work from an administration subnet at 10.0.9.0/24, and its servers sit in a server subnet at 10.0.5.0/24. The boundary is a stateless packet filter that holds an ordered list of rules. The filter compares a flow against the rules from the top of the list downwards, and the first rule whose source, destination and port all match the flow decides the action; no later rule is consulted, whether the action was ALLOW or DENY. The last rule in the list is the catch-all.

The administrator has been asked to allow the system administrators to reach the servers over SSH from the administration subnet, while denying every other flow that enters the server subnet. The rules currently in the filter, and two flows that were captured at the boundary, are shown in the figure. The server subnet holds the host 10.0.5.20, which runs the public web service, and the host 10.0.5.31, which the administrators manage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the rule table, determine the action the filter takes for each of the two flows in the figure, and name the number of the rule that decides each one. For each flow, show why every rule above the deciding rule fails to match it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why rule 3 never decides the action for any flow at all, whatever its source address and whatever port it carries. Your answer must refer to the destination pattern in rule 3, to the destination pattern in the rule above it, and to the position of that rule in the list, and must state the property of the two patterns that makes the outcome unavoidable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the smallest change to the table that restores the administrator's intention, and evaluate one security consequence of making that change. Your answer should state how many hosts in the server subnet the restored rule would reach, explain what the rule grants to every device on the administration subnet, and state whether rule 4 should be kept.

questions.answer:
(a) Flow 1 runs from 203.0.113.7 to 10.0.5.20 on port 443. Rule 1 has a destination of exactly 10.0.5.20 and a port of 443, and its source is a wildcard, so it matches and the action is ALLOW (A1). Rule 2 is never consulted, because the filter stops at the first match and rule 1 sits above it.

Flow 2 runs from 10.0.9.14 to 10.0.5.31 on port 22. Rule 1 does not match it: the destination 10.0.5.31 is a different host from 10.0.5.20, and the port 22 is a different port from 443 (A1). Rule 2 has a destination of 10.0.5.0/24 and a port wildcard, so it matches any host in the server subnet on any port. The address 10.0.5.31 lies in 10.0.5.0/24, so rule 2 matches and the action is DENY (A1). Rule 3 is not consulted, even though its source, destination and port all describe flow 2 exactly.

(b) Rule 3 requires a destination in 10.0.5.0/24 and a port of 22, from a source in 10.0.9.0/24. Rule 2 requires a destination in 10.0.5.0/24, and its source and port are both wildcards (A1). Every flow that can match rule 3 therefore also matches rule 2: the set of destinations rule 3 accepts is the whole server subnet, and that is exactly the set of destinations rule 2 accepts, so rule 3 adds no destination that rule 2 does not already cover (A1).

Rule 2 also accepts every source and every port, so it cannot fail on a flow that rule 3 would have accepted. Since rule 2 sits above rule 3 in the list, the filter reaches rule 2 first for every such flow, matches it, and stops (A1). The property that makes this unavoidable is that rule 2's match set is a superset of rule 3's, and a superset earlier in a first-match list makes the rule below it unreachable. It is not a configuration error that a validation check would catch by looking at rule 3 alone: rule 3 is well formed, and it is only the pair of rules and their order that makes it dead (A1).

(c) The smallest change is to exchange the positions of rule 2 and rule 3, so that the SSH allowance is evaluated before the blanket denial (A1). After the exchange, flow 2 is matched by rule 3 and is ALLOWed, while flow 1 is still matched by rule 1 and unaffected, and a flow into the server subnet from anywhere other than the administration subnet still falls through to rule 2 and is denied (A1).

The security consequence is that the restored rule is written over a subnet, not over a host. Its destination is 10.0.5.0/24, which is 254 usable addresses, and its source is 10.0.9.0/24, which is another 254 (A1). The administrator wanted the system administrators to manage 10.0.5.31; the rule as written grants SSH access from every device on the administration subnet to every host in the server subnet, including the public web host at 10.0.5.20. One compromised workstation on the administration network therefore has an SSH path to the whole server estate, and the workstation does not need any privilege beyond an address in the subnet. Narrowing rule 3's destination to the hosts that actually need managing, or pairing it with multifactor authentication, would keep the intent while removing the reach (A1).

Rule 4 should be kept. It is the default deny, and it is the reason the table fails closed: anything that matches no earlier rule is dropped. Removing it would leave unmatched traffic with no decision, which in most implementations means it is permitted, so the table would move from denying by default to allowing by default and every flow the other rules do not name would be admitted. The correct reading of rule 4 is that it is not redundant with rule 2; rule 2 denies the server subnet, and rule 4 denies everything else, including flows to the rest of the estate (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) 3 marks. One mark for flow 1 decided by rule 1 with the action ALLOW. One mark for flow 2 decided by rule 2 with the action DENY. One mark for showing that rule 1 fails on flow 2 because the destination host and the port both differ, and that rule 2 therefore matches before rule 3 is reached. A candidate who answers flow 2 with rule 3 has read the rule that mentions SSH and has not evaluated the list; no marks for that flow.

(b) 4 marks. One mark for stating that rule 3's destination set is the whole server subnet. One mark for stating that rule 2's destination set is the same whole subnet, so rule 3 adds nothing to it. One mark for stating that rule 2 is evaluated first and that the filter stops at the first match. One mark for naming the general property, that a rule whose match set contains another rule's match set makes the other rule unreachable when it is placed above it. A candidate who says only 'rule 3 is never reached because rule 2 catches everything first' earns two of the four marks; the other two require the pattern comparison and the general statement.

Accept 'shadowed', 'unreachable', 'dead rule' or an equivalent phrase for the final mark.

(c) 5 marks. One mark for the smallest change, which is to swap rules 2 and 3, or equivalently to move rule 3 above rule 2. One mark for confirming that the swap leaves flow 1 decided by rule 1 and still denies flows into the server subnet from elsewhere. One mark for the count of 254 usable hosts at each end of the restored rule. One mark for the consequence: the rule reaches the public web host as well as the managed host, and every device on the administration subnet inherits it, so one compromised workstation gains an SSH path to the whole server estate. One mark for stating that rule 4 should be kept and giving the reason, that it is the default deny and removing it would allow unmatched traffic.

A candidate who proposes adding a new rule above rule 2 that names only 10.0.5.31 has changed the intention, which was to allow the whole server subnet. Accept it only if the candidate states that it narrows the intention and explains why that is acceptable.

Accept 'moving rule 3 up' and 'swapping 2 and 3' as the same answer. Do not accept 'change rule 2 to allow SSH', which breaks the denial for every other source.
questions.explanation:
A stateless packet filter is an ordered list, and its semantics are first-match. Two consequences follow that are easy to state and easy to get wrong. The first is that the order carries meaning that no individual rule expresses: the same four rules in a different order are a different filter. The second is that a rule can be well formed, correct in its own fields, and still never decide anything, because a rule above it matches everything it would have matched. That condition is called shadowing, and it is the reason a firewall audit compares rules in pairs rather than reading them one at a time.

The shadowing here is exact rather than partial. Rule 3's destination is 10.0.5.0/24 and rule 2's destination is 10.0.5.0/24, so the two destination sets are not merely overlapping, they are identical; rule 2 is broader only in that its source and port are wildcards. A candidate can see this without enumerating addresses, and the verification does enumerate them, all 256 of them, to confirm that no host in the server subnet escapes rule 2's pattern.

The item is written so that the wrong answer is the one that looks most like diligence. A candidate who reads the table and looks for the rule about SSH finds rule 3, and rule 3 says exactly what the administrator intended. The mistake is not misreading the rule; it is treating a list as a set. The two flows in the figure are chosen so that the list and the set give different answers: flow 2 is precisely the flow rule 3 was written for, and the list denies it.

The final part makes the repair carry a cost, which is what turns the item from a puzzle into an evaluation. Restoring the intention is one line of reordering, and it simultaneously widens the reach of the allowance from one host to a subnet of 254, because the rule was always written over a subnet and the shadowing was hiding that. So the correct answer has to hold two things at once: the rule was dead, and reviving it grants more than the administrator thought it did. That is the sense in which rule-based filtering has limitations as well as strengths, which is the language the guide uses for this node.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A3.3 Database programming (A3.3.6 describe how transactions maintain data integrity in a database, including the role of atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability to ensure reliable processing of transactions, and the transaction control language commands BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT and ROLLBACK)
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Two transfers that interleave so that the second reads the balance before the first commits, and the committed value is short by exactly the first transfer
questions.challenge_mechanism: Nothing in the timeline is wrong. Both transactions read a value that was correct when it was read, both compute their new value correctly from what they read, both commit successfully, and the stored balance is still a hundred short of the truth. There is no bad statement to find, because the fault is in the ordering rather than in any of the operations, and an ordering fault leaves no trace in the data to inspect afterwards.
questions.question:
A savings account holds a balance of 500. Two transfers into the account are submitted at almost the same moment: one adds 100 and one adds 50. Each transfer is written as a transaction that reads the balance, computes the new balance from the value it read, writes that value back, and commits. The application does not use a lock, and the database engine is running at an isolation level that permits the two transactions to interleave.

The figure shows what the engine actually did, as an ordered list of operations. Each operation is labelled with the transaction that issued it and the moment it was issued. Nothing in the figure has been simplified: this is the whole of both transactions, and both of them commit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the timeline, state the balance that each of the two transactions reads and the balance that each of them writes. Determine the balance that is left in the account once both transactions have committed, and state which of the two COMMIT statements fixes that value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the balance that would remain if the two transfers had run one after the other, and show that both possible orders give the same result. State the amount by which the interleaved execution has lost. Name the ACID property whose role this interleaving has defeated, and name one of the other three properties that this same interleaving has not defeated, justifying each of your two answers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A developer proposes to change nothing in the application, to rely on ROLLBACK to undo any damage, and to allow both transactions to run for longer so that they overlap more often. Evaluate that proposal. Your answer should state what ROLLBACK can and cannot recover in this timeline, identify the smallest change to the timeline that removes the loss, and reach a judgement on whether this anomaly can be prevented using transaction control commands alone.

questions.answer:
(a) The first SELECT is issued by the first transaction at t1 and returns 500. The second SELECT is issued by the second transaction at t3 and also returns 500, because the first transaction has not yet written anything at that moment (A1). The first transaction writes $500 + 100 = 600$ at t4, and the second writes $500 + 50 = 550$ at t6 (A1). The last COMMIT is the second transaction's, at t7, and it fixes the stored balance at 550 (A1). The first transaction's 600 is not in the database any more: the second transaction wrote over it.

(b) Run in either serial order, the arithmetic gives the same answer. First then second: the first reads 500 and writes 600, then the second reads 600 and writes $600 + 50 = 650$. Second then first: the second reads 500 and writes 550, then the first reads 550 and writes $550 + 100 = 650$ (M1). Both orders give 650, which is what makes 650 the correct result rather than merely one possible result (A1).

The interleaved execution has left 550, so the loss is $650 - 550 = 100$ (A1). That is exactly the amount the first transaction added, which is what a lost update looks like: one transaction's write is entirely overwritten by another's, and the update that is lost is the earlier one.

The property whose role has been defeated is isolation (A1). Isolation is what guarantees that the result of running transactions concurrently is the same as the result of running them in some serial order, and here the concurrent result of 550 matches neither serial order.

Atomicity has not been defeated. Each transaction did what atomicity requires: the first transaction's read and write both took effect and it committed as a unit, and the second's did the same. Atomicity is about a transaction not being half-applied, and neither transaction was half-applied; the first was applied in full and then overwritten in full by a later transaction, which is an ordering fault and not a failure of atomicity. Durability has not been defeated either: both COMMIT statements were honoured and both transactions' effects were persisted, and the persisted value is wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with losing committed data. Either answer earns the mark, provided the candidate distinguishes it from isolation.

(c) ROLLBACK undoes the writes of the transaction that issues it, and only while that transaction has not yet committed. In this timeline there is nothing left for it to undo (A1). By t7 both transactions have committed, so neither can be rolled back: a rollback of the first transaction is refused because it has already committed, and a rollback of the second would remove the 550 and leave the account at 500, which is worse, not better. The value the first transaction computed, 600, was overwritten inside the second transaction's write and is no longer held anywhere the database can reach. ROLLBACK recovers a transaction that has failed; it cannot recover a value that a later committed transaction has already replaced.

Making the transactions run for longer, so that they overlap more often, makes the anomaly more likely rather than less. The loss happened because the second transaction's read fell between the first transaction's read and its COMMIT. Widening the interval between a transaction's read and its commit widens exactly the window in which another transaction can read the old value, so the proposal increases the frequency of the fault it is offered as a defence against (A1).

The smallest change to the timeline is to move the second transaction's read so that it happens after the first transaction's COMMIT, that is from t3 to after t5 (A1). If the second transaction reads after t5 it reads 600, and it then writes $600 + 50 = 650$, which is the correct result. Nothing else needs to change: both transactions keep their structure, both still commit, and no statement is rewritten. The change is a change of ordering, and it corresponds to a real mechanism, which is to make the second transaction wait until the first has finished, whether by taking a lock on the row before reading it or by raising the isolation level so that the engine takes one on the transaction's behalf (A1).

The judgement is that this anomaly cannot be prevented using transaction control commands alone (A1). The commands the guide lists are BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT and ROLLBACK, and between them they let a candidate start a transaction, finish it successfully, or abandon it. None of them constrains when another transaction may read. The fault is in the interleaving, and the interleaving is controlled by locking and by the isolation level, which are properties of how the transaction is declared and of how the engine schedules it rather than commands that a developer issues. A candidate who answers that ROLLBACK can be used to detect and retry the second transaction should be credited for the retry idea, but must also be asked to say what triggers the rollback, since nothing in this timeline fails and so nothing raises an error for the application to catch.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) 3 marks. One mark for both reads giving 500. One mark for the two written values, 600 and 550, each computed from the value that transaction actually read. One mark for the final committed balance of 550 and for attributing it to the second transaction's COMMIT. A candidate who answers 650 has added the transfers together without following the timeline; no marks for that part.

(b) 4 marks. One mark for showing both serial orders, 600 then 650 and 550 then 650, and stating that they agree. One mark for the loss of 100 and for identifying it as the first transaction's increment. One mark for isolation as the property defeated, with a reason that refers to the serial-order guarantee. One mark for naming atomicity or durability as preserved, with a reason. A candidate who names consistency as defeated should be credited only if the answer states the invariant that was broken, namely that the two transfers must both be reflected in the balance.

Do not accept 'atomicity is violated' for the final mark: both transactions committed as units, and the failure is in the ordering.

(c) 6 marks. One mark for stating that ROLLBACK cannot act here because both transactions have committed. One mark for stating that a rollback of the second transaction would make the balance worse rather than better. One mark for the observation that making the transactions overlap more often widens the read-to-commit window and increases the fault rate. One mark for the smallest change, which is to move the second read to after the first COMMIT, giving a write of 650. One mark for naming the mechanism, a row lock or a raised isolation level. One mark for the judgement that transaction control commands alone cannot prevent the anomaly, with the reason that none of BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT and ROLLBACK constrains when another transaction may read.

A candidate who proposes a retry loop should keep the first four marks if the reordering is also given, but must be asked what would trigger the retry, since no statement in this timeline raises an error.
questions.explanation:
This is the classic lost update, and it is worth being precise about why it is hard. The two transactions are individually correct. Each reads the balance, each computes a new balance from what it read, each writes, each commits. There is no statement a reviewer could point at and call wrong. The defect is entirely in the ordering: the second transaction's read falls after the first transaction's read and before the first transaction's COMMIT, which is the one interval in which the value it reads is about to be superseded.

That is why the figure is given as an ordered list rather than as a description. The candidate cannot answer by pattern-matching the word 'transaction' to a list of ACID properties; the properties have to be used to predict an outcome, and then checked against the arithmetic. The item is a harder route to exactly the content the guide names, which is the role of isolation in maintaining integrity.

The loss is exactly 100, the first transaction's increment, and that is not a coincidence of the numbers chosen. When one transaction overwrites another's write with a value computed from a stale read, the surviving value is the later transaction's read plus the later transaction's increment, so the difference from the correct serial result is the earlier transaction's increment in full. A candidate who notices this has understood the mechanism rather than the example, and the answer says so.

Part (c) is written so that the two plausible remedies are both wrong. ROLLBACK cannot help because by the time anyone notices, both transactions have committed, and rolling back the second would discard a correct 50 to remove a wrong 100. Making the transactions longer makes the window wider and the fault commoner. What actually fixes it is a change of ordering, which is to say a lock or an isolation level, and the judgement the part asks for is that the transaction control commands the guide lists do not reach that far. That is a real and examinable point: BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT and ROLLBACK delimit a transaction, and they do not schedule it.

The item deliberately avoids the terms 'dirty read' and 'non-repeatable read', which belong to a finer-grained taxonomy than the guide asks for. Everything the candidate needs is in the timeline and in the four properties named by A3.3.6.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Add the two transfers to the starting balance, or follow each transaction's own arithmetic in isolation, and report the final balance as 650 on the grounds that both transactions read a correct value, both computed correctly and both committed
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The second transaction computes its write from the value it read at t3, which is 500, and its write of 550 replaces the first transaction's committed 600 wholesale, so the committed balance is 100 short and the shortfall is invisible in every individual statement
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A committed balance of 650 with both transactions reported as successful, which is the sum of the two increments and is the value neither serial order of the operations as written can produce

verification.method: Both serial orders are evaluated independently and compared with the interleaved order, so the loss is derived rather than asserted; the lost amount is then checked against the first transaction's increment, which is the value the mechanism predicts. The read and write values are recomputed from the timeline's stated operations, and the ordering that causes the anomaly is confirmed by comparing the position of the second read with the position of the first commit.
solution_skeleton: Read the two read values and the two written values from the timeline.
Take the value fixed by the last COMMIT as the committed balance.
Evaluate both serial orders and check that they agree.
Compare the serial result with the committed value to obtain the loss.
Attribute the loss to the ordering of the read and the commit.
Test whether any listed command can change that ordering.

questions.syllabus_ref: A3.4 Alternative databases and data warehouses (HL only) (A3.4.2 explain the primary objectives of data warehouses in data management and business intelligence, including the roles of append-only data, time-variant data and non-volatile data, and the role of data optimized for query performance)
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Reading an append-only load table whose rows supersede one another, where the two natural wrong totals err in opposite directions
questions.challenge_mechanism: Two defensible ways of adding up an append-only table are both wrong, and they are wrong in opposite directions. Adding every row counts a row that a later row has replaced; adding only the rows from the most recent load drops a row from an earlier load that is still current. Neither error cancels the other, so the correct total is neither of the two and is not their average, and the two figures are close enough to each other that a candidate who checks one against the other will conclude they agree.
questions.question:
A retail group loads its sales data into a warehouse every night. The warehouse never updates a row and never deletes one: each night's load appends new rows, and the table's whole history is still present. The same product can appear in more than one night's load, and more than one source system can report on the same product in the same night.

Two rules govern how the table is read. A row supersedes any earlier row that carries the same product and the same source, so only the newest row for a given product and source is current. Rows from different sources are not alternatives to one another and are added together, because they describe different parts of the same sale. The table is shown in the figure, together with the night on which each row was written.

The operations director has asked for the current total units and the current total revenue, and has been given two different answers by two analysts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of rows the table holds, the number of distinct products it holds, and the number of distinct combinations of product and source. Hence state how many of the rows have been superseded, and explain why an append-only table holds more rows than it holds current facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the current total units and the current total revenue, applying the reading rules given above. State how many of the four rows contribute to your total, and explain for each row that does not contribute why it does not.

parts.label: c
parts.text: One analyst adds units and revenue over every row in the table. The other finds the greatest load date in the table and adds only the rows that carry it. Calculate the units and revenue that each analyst reports, and state the direction and the size of the error in each against the correct total. Explain why the correct total is neither of the two answers nor the average of them. Then reach a judgement on which of the two errors the warehouse's own design makes easier to detect, and why.

questions.answer:
(a) The table holds four rows. It holds two distinct products, P1 and P2, and three distinct combinations of product and source: P1 from the till, P1 from adjustments, and P2 from the till (A1). One of the four rows has therefore been superseded, since four rows describe three current facts (A1).

An append-only table holds more rows than current facts because it never overwrites. When a source restates its figures for a product, the correction is written as a new row rather than applied to the old one, so both the superseded row and the row that supersedes it remain in the table (A1). This is the property the guide calls time-variant: the table records what was believed at each point in time, not only what is believed now, and the earlier belief is preserved rather than erased.

(b) The current rows are found by taking, for each combination of product and source, the row with the greatest load date.

- For P1 from the till there are two rows. The row written on 1 April carries 100 units and 2000 revenue, and the row written on 8 April carries 90 units and 1800 revenue. The later row is current, so the April 1 row does not contribute (M1).
- For P1 from adjustments there is one row, written on 1 April, carrying 50 units and 1000 revenue. Nothing supersedes it, so it is current and it contributes (A1).
- For P2 from the till there is one row, written on 8 April, carrying 40 units and 800 revenue. It is current and it contributes (A1).

The current totals are therefore $90 + 50 + 40 = 180$ units and $1800 + 1000 + 800 = 3600$ revenue (A1). Three of the four rows contribute. The row that does not is the 1 April row for P1 from the till, and it does not because the 8 April row from the same source for the same product supersedes it.

(c) Adding every row gives $100 + 50 + 90 + 40 = 280$ units and $2000 + 1000 + 1800 + 800 = 5600$ revenue (M1). The error is an over-statement of 100 units and 2000 revenue, and it is exactly the superseded row counted as though it were still current (A1).

Taking the greatest load date, which is 8 April, and adding only the rows that carry it gives $90 + 40 = 130$ units and $1800 + 800 = 2600$ revenue (M1). The error here is an under-statement of 50 units and 1000 revenue, and it is caused by dropping the P1 adjustments row, which was written on 1 April and has never been superseded (A1).

The correct total is 180 units and 3600 revenue, so it is neither 280 and 5600 nor 130 and 2600. It is also not the average of the two revenue figures, which would be $(2600 + 5600)/2 = 4100$ (A1). The two errors do not offset each other because they are not errors of the same kind. The first counts a row that should be excluded; the second excludes a row that should be counted. They happen to be different rows of different sizes, so nothing makes their effects equal and nothing makes them cancel. Treating two wrong answers as bracketing the right one is only sound when the errors are known to be symmetric, and nothing here establishes that (A1).

The judgement is that the warehouse's design makes the first error the easier of the two to detect (A1). The over-statement is caused by a row that is still physically present and still carries its original load date, so the row that should have been excluded can be found by comparing load dates within a product and source: wherever two rows share a product and a source, the older one is superseded, and the table itself supplies the evidence. The under-statement is caused by a row that has been silently omitted. Nothing in the data records the omission, because the row that was left out is indistinguishable from the rows that were correctly left out, and the query that produced the figure returns a smaller number with no indication that anything is missing (A1). An append-only design therefore makes the error of counting too much self-diagnosing and the error of counting too little invisible, which is the reason the reading rule has to be stated explicitly rather than inferred from the data.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) 3 marks. One mark for four rows, two products and three product-and-source combinations. One mark for one superseded row. One mark for the reason, that the table appends rather than overwrites so a restatement leaves both the old row and the new one in place.

(b) 4 marks. One mark for identifying the 8 April P1 till row as the current row for its pair and giving 90 and 1800 for it. One mark for keeping the 1 April P1 adjustments row and giving 50 and 1000 for it, with the reason that no later row from the same source supersedes it. One mark for the P2 row, 40 and 800. One mark for the totals, 180 units and 3600 revenue, together with the statement that three of the four rows contribute. A candidate who gives 130 and 2600 has applied the greatest-load-date rule instead of the per-pair rule and loses the second and fourth marks.

Accept 180 and 3600 in either order. Do not accept a total that includes the 1 April P1 till row, however it is justified, since the rule given in the figure supersedes it.

(c) 6 marks. One mark for 280 units and 5600 revenue. One mark for the direction and size of that error, an over-statement of 100 and 2000, attributed to the superseded row. One mark for 130 units and 2600 revenue. One mark for the direction and size of that error, an under-statement of 50 and 1000, attributed to the dropped adjustments row. One mark for rejecting the average of 4100 with a reason, namely that the two errors are of different kinds and are not symmetric. One mark for the judgement that the over-statement is the detectable one, because the superseded row is still present and can be identified by comparing load dates within a product and source, while the under-statement leaves no trace.

A candidate who says the two errors cancel, or who averages them without argument, loses the fifth mark. A candidate who reaches 3600 by a correct route and then states that the average is 4100 and therefore wrong earns that mark even without the detectability judgement.
questions.explanation:
An append-only table is a log of what was reported, not a picture of what is true. That is its strength and it is also the reason it cannot be summed naively. Every aggregate over such a table has to be paired with a rule that says which rows are current, and the rule has to be applied at the grain of the thing that can be restated. Here the grain is the pair of product and source, because the till and the adjustments ledger report on the same product independently and neither supersedes the other.

The two wrong answers are the two ways of getting the grain wrong. Summing every row applies no rule at all. Filtering on the greatest load date applies a rule at the wrong grain: it treats a load as the unit that supersedes, so a source that did not report on the most recent night disappears from the total. The second error is the more interesting one because the query looks principled. It contains a deliberate filter, it produces a smaller and therefore apparently safer number, and it is wrong because the thing being superseded is a row and not a night.

The two errors run in opposite directions, which is what makes the item a test of reasoning rather than of arithmetic. A candidate who computes both and finds one high and one low may be tempted to conclude that the truth lies between them, and the average of 4100 is not the truth. Bracket-and-average is only valid when the two errors are known to be of comparable size and opposite sign, and here they are 2000 and 1000 in opposite directions, which is a ratio of two to one and not a symmetry.

The final judgement is about the design rather than the query. Because the warehouse never deletes, the superseded row is still there and can be found by a rule that the table itself supports; the error of counting it is therefore a rule that can be checked against the data. The error of dropping a row leaves the data consistent with the wrong answer, so no amount of inspection of the table will reveal it. That asymmetry is the practical reason a warehouse specification states the currency rule rather than leaving it to be inferred, and it is the point the part is asking the candidate to reach.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: a nightly-loaded retail warehouse whose rows supersede one another across two independent source systems, rather than a question about what a data warehouse is for. Given and asked: the raw append-only table is given and the candidate must derive the current totals from it, so the currency rule has to be applied rather than described. Reasoning chain: the final part requires the candidate to reject the average of two wrong answers and to reason about which error the storage design makes visible.
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-level Computer Science and US AP Computer Science Principles: data warehouses, append-only loads and slowly changing data (structure adapted; all rows, dates and figures are original)

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Add the units and the revenue of every row in the table, on the grounds that the warehouse is described as holding the whole history and that each row is a record of something that was genuinely reported, and report 280 units and 5600 revenue
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: A row that a later row has superseded is no longer current even though it is still present, so summing every row counts the 1 April P1 till row twice over: once as itself and once as the history the 8 April row replaced, over-stating revenue by exactly 2000
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: 280 units and 5600 revenue, which is the sum of the whole table and counts a superseded row as current, and which a candidate who then compares it with the 130 and 2600 produced by the load-date filter will find only 100 and 1000 away from it

verification.method: The current rows are derived by grouping the table on product and source and taking the greatest load date in each group, then summing the surviving rows, so the totals are computed from the rule rather than asserted. Both wrong totals are computed independently, their errors are checked against the superseded row's own figures, and the average of the two is compared with the correct total to confirm it does not coincide.
solution_skeleton: Group the rows by product and source.
Take the greatest load date within each group and keep only those rows.
Sum the surviving rows to obtain the current totals.
Compute both wrong totals and express each error against the current total.
Compare the correct total with the average of the two wrong totals.
Reason about which error the append-only design leaves a trace of.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A4.4 Ethical considerations (A4.4.1 discuss the ethical implications of machine learning in real-world scenarios, including accountability, consent, privacy and transparency, and the challenges posed by biases in training data)
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Withdrawn consent against a model that was trained before the withdrawal, where deleting the records changes the corpus but not the model
questions.challenge_mechanism: Deleting the records is necessary and it is not sufficient, and the two facts look like the same fact. The corpus after the deletion contains none of the withdrawn records, so a check of the corpus passes; the model was trained while they were still there, so a check of the model fails. The team's evidence and the team's obligation are about different objects, and the size of the deletion makes the gap easy to miss.
questions.question:
A clinic uses a machine-learning model to prioritise referrals. The model has been through two runs. The first trained a model from scratch on the whole corpus as it stood at that date. The second produced the model that is currently deployed by continuing to train the first model on records that had arrived since.

Patients consent to their records being used for research, and consent may be withdrawn at any time. A group of patients has now withdrawn consent, and their records must no longer be used. The clinic has deleted those records from the corpus and has asked for advice on what else, if anything, is required before the deployed model can be described as compliant.

The figure gives the dates of the two runs, the size of the corpus at each point, the number of records withdrawn, and how those withdrawn records are distributed between the two runs. The clinic intends to describe the deployed model as compliant once the deletions are complete.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the figure, determine the number of records the corpus holds immediately before the deletions and immediately after them, and determine how many of the withdrawn records were used by the run that trained the first model and how many by the run that produced the deployed model.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine how many of the withdrawn records were never used in any training run at all, and explain what your answer implies for the two models that have already been produced. Your answer should state what deleting the records changes about those models and what it does not change.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The team proposes to continue training the deployed model on the remaining records and then to describe it as compliant. Evaluate that proposal. Your answer should state how many records a model retrained from scratch would be trained on, express the reduction in training data as a percentage of the corpus the deployed model was built from, explain why that percentage is small while the compliance question is not, and reach a judgement on which remedy the withdrawals require.

questions.answer:
(a) Before the deletions the corpus holds the 48 000 records the first run trained on plus the 12 000 that arrived afterwards, which is 60 000 (A1). After the 900 withdrawn records are deleted it holds $60\,000 - 900 = 59\,100$ (A1).

The withdrawn records are not all in the same run. Of the 900, 620 had already been used by the run that trained the first model, because they were part of the 48 000. The remaining 280 arrived with the 12 000 and were used by the run that produced the deployed model (A1).

(b) The two runs between them used $620 + 280 = 900$ of the withdrawn records, so the number that were never used in any training run is $900 - 900 = 0$ (A1). Every withdrawn record contributed to at least one training run.

The implication is that both models were trained on data that must no longer be used. The first model was trained on a corpus that contained 620 of the withdrawn records, so its parameters were computed in part from them (A1). The deployed model was produced by continuing to train that first model, so it inherits everything the first model learned and adds what it learned from the remaining 280; its parameters are therefore a function of all 900 (A1).

Deleting the records changes the corpus and does not change either model. What it changes is what the clinic holds and what any future training run would be able to use. What it does not change is what the models already contain: a trained model is a set of parameter values, and those values were fixed at the moment the run finished. They do not refer back to the corpus, and they are not recomputed when the corpus changes. Removing a row from the corpus is therefore not the same operation as removing that row's influence from the model, and only the first of the two has happened (A1).

(c) A model retrained from scratch would be trained on the 59 100 records that remain, because a run that starts from an untrained model and uses only the current corpus would have no access to the 900 (A1).

The reduction in training data is $900/60\,000 = 0.015$, which is 1.5 per cent (A1). That is a small number, and the reason it does not settle the question is that it measures the wrong thing. It compares the size of the remaining corpus with the size of the old one, and it would only be relevant if the obligation were to avoid training on a large fraction of the data. The obligation is to avoid using the withdrawn records at all, and by that measure the withdrawn records are not 1.5 per cent of anything: all 900 of them were used, so 100 per cent of the withdrawn records are represented in the deployed model. A proportion can be made to look small by choosing a large denominator, and the denominator here is irrelevant to whether the obligation has been met (A1).

The proposal to continue training the deployed model on the remaining records does not meet it. Continuing to train starts from the deployed model's existing parameters, and those parameters already encode the withdrawn records. Further training on the remaining 59 100 records moves the parameters towards what those records imply, but it provides no mechanism that removes the influence the earlier records had on the point it started from. In the limit, training for long enough on the remaining records would reduce the dependence on the withdrawn ones, but the proposal does not say how long, and there is no measurement in the figure or in the proposal that would show when the influence had gone (A1).

The judgement is that the withdrawals require the model to be retrained from scratch on the remaining corpus, or rebuilt by a method that can demonstrate the removal of the withdrawn records' influence and is accepted as doing so (A1). Retraining from scratch is the remedy that follows from the evidence in the figure, because it is the only one of the two proposals whose training data can be stated exactly, and the statement is that it contains none of the 900. It is also the more expensive of the two, and the cost is the reason the proposal in the question was made. The clinic should also record what happened rather than only what was done, since the models were trained on the withdrawn data and any account of the deployed system that omits this is incomplete: accountability here means being able to say which corpus produced the model that is making decisions about patients, and that is a question about the past that deleting records now cannot answer (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) 3 marks. One mark for 60 000 before the deletions. One mark for 59 100 after them. One mark for splitting the 900 into 620 used by the first run and 280 used by the second. A candidate who gives 48 000 and 12 000 as the two corpora without combining them has read the figure but has not answered the question; award the third mark only if the 620 and 280 split is also given.

(b) 4 marks. One mark for zero, that is for establishing that every withdrawn record was used. One mark for stating that the first model was trained on 620 of them. One mark for stating that the deployed model inherits the first model's parameters and adds the 280, so it depends on all 900. One mark for the distinction between deleting records from the corpus and removing their influence from a model whose parameters were fixed when the run finished.

The fourth mark is the one that separates a candidate who has understood the mechanism from one who has understood the vocabulary. A candidate who says only 'the model must be retrained' without explaining why deletion is insufficient earns three marks.

(c) 5 marks. One mark for 59 100 as the corpus for a retrained model. One mark for the reduction expressed as 1.5 per cent, or as 0.015, of 60 000. One mark for the explanation that the percentage measures the size of the corpus rather than the compliance question, together with the observation that 100 per cent of the withdrawn records were used. One mark for explaining why continuing to train from the existing parameters does not remove the earlier records' influence. One mark for a judgement that names retraining from scratch, or an accepted method that can demonstrate removal of the influence, as the remedy the withdrawals require, and that acknowledges the cost or the difficulty of the choice.

Accept a candidate who argues for an approved machine-unlearning procedure, provided the answer states that the removal of influence has to be demonstrated rather than assumed. Do not accept a candidate who argues that deleting the records is sufficient, however the argument is framed, because part (b) has already established that every withdrawn record was used.

Accept either order for the 620 and 280 split. Accept 'retrain' without the phrase 'from scratch' only if the answer makes clear that the starting point is an untrained model and the training set is the remaining corpus.
questions.explanation:
The gap this item is built on is the gap between a dataset and a model trained on it. A dataset is a collection that can be edited: a row can be removed and the collection is then smaller. A trained model is a set of parameter values produced by a process that read the dataset once, and the values do not contain the dataset. They contain whatever the training process made of it. So an obligation that says 'do not use this record' cannot be discharged by editing the collection, because the use has already happened and its result is elsewhere.

The figure is built so that the arithmetic makes this concrete rather than theoretical. The withdrawal is split across the two runs, 620 and 280, so that neither model can be cleared by looking at one of them. The second run is a continuation of the first, so its dependence on the first run's data is not a matter of degree: the deployed model's parameters are a function of everything the first model saw. And the deletion is 1.5 per cent of the corpus, which is small enough that a team looking at the size of the change would conclude it had done something minor and sufficient.

The percentage is the trap. It is computed correctly and it answers a question nobody asked. The obligation is about a set of records, and the fraction of those records that were used is 100 per cent, which is the figure that matters. The item asks the candidate to hold both numbers at once and to say which one bears on compliance, which is the same discipline the guide asks for when it lists transparency and accountability alongside consent as ethical issues for machine learning.

The judgement is deliberately left with two acceptable routes. Retraining from scratch is the route the evidence in the figure supports directly, because the training set of the new model can be stated exactly and it contains none of the 900. An accepted unlearning method is the other route, and it is admitted only with the condition that removal of the influence has to be demonstrated, which keeps the item honest about a methodology that is still developing. What the item does not admit is the third route, which is to continue training and hope, and the reason is that there is no measurement in the problem that would show when the hope had been realised.

Nothing in the item requires knowledge outside the guide. Consent, accountability, transparency and privacy are all named in A4.4.1, and the machine-learning concepts used here, training and continued training, are the ordinary vocabulary of the topic rather than an additional technique.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: a clinical model that has been deployed across two training runs, with a consent withdrawal that has to be assessed against what has already happened, rather than a discussion of why consent matters. Given and asked: the dates, the corpus sizes and the split of the withdrawals are given in a figure, and the candidate is asked to determine what the deletion does and does not change rather than to state a principle. Reasoning chain: the final part requires the candidate to reject a percentage that is correctly computed but irrelevant, and to justify a remedy that is more expensive than the one proposed.
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-level Computer Science and US AP Computer Science Principles, with the ethical vocabulary of the IB computer science guide A4.4.1: consent, accountability and transparency in machine learning (structure adapted; all dates, corpus sizes and the withdrawal split are original)

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Delete the 900 withdrawn records from the corpus, observe that the corpus now contains none of them, and treat the deployed model as compliant on the grounds that the data it was built from has been removed and that the deletion is only 1.5 per cent of the corpus
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The model's compliance depends on when it was trained relative to the withdrawal, and that fact is not visible in the corpus the team is inspecting: the parameters were fixed before the deletion and are never recomputed, so every one of the 900 records is still represented in a model whose training data no longer contains them
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The deployed model described as compliant once the 900 records are deleted, supported by the observation that the removal is 1.5 per cent of the corpus, which is a correct calculation of the change in the corpus and says nothing about the influence that remains in the model

verification.method: The corpus sizes are recomputed from the two load dates and checked against the deletion, and the withdrawal is split between the runs and checked to account for all 900 records, which is what establishes that none of them was unused. The reduction is computed both as a fraction of the original corpus and as the fraction of the withdrawn records that were used, so that the two measures can be compared directly and the item's claim about which one bears on compliance can be checked.
solution_skeleton: Read the two corpus sizes and the withdrawal count from the figure.
Split the withdrawals between the two runs and check they sum to the total.
Establish that no withdrawn record went unused by either run.
Compare the size of the deletion with the obligation it is meant to meet.
Separate the corpus, which the deletion changes, from the parameters it does not.
Choose the remedy whose training set can be stated exactly.
